Turn the wheel until the letter reads true, then seal your answer.
Look at the wheel, boy. Somewhere among its stops is the one number that makes this letter speak.
This is old Caesar's trick: every letter walked forward the same number of stops. Turn the outer ring and watch the words wake.
Turn it one notch at a time and read the first few words aloud. The moment they sound like speech instead of noise, seal it.
The Rusted Wheel
Read the tally before you spend blood turning the wheel by guesswork.
Don't spin the wheel blind, it costs you now. Look at the Tally Scroll first and see which bar stands tallest.
In any honest letter one letter does most of the work. Find that tallest bar and count its distance to what it should be.
Read the tallest column as the commonest letter in plain speech, then turn the wheel that many stops before you spend another drop.
Thirteen Turns
Name each note's trick, then say what truly kept them secret.
Three notes, three little tricks. Look for one that never changes a letter's shape, only its place in the alphabet.
One trick always adds thirteen and undoes itself if you do it twice. The other flips the alphabet on its head, first for last.
Name each note's trick, then ask yourself plainly what is left to hide once the trick itself is known. Answer that, and seal.
What truly protects these three notes?
The number of turns given to the wheel
The Court's wax seal pressed on each letter
Nothing, once the trick itself is known

Reeve Bassett,
The new moon falls in nine nights. See the tithe-house at Reedmouth aired and swept, the rushes changed, and the rotten planking by the door replaced before the carts arrive. Count every head in the village yourself, cellar and loft besides. Last season's tally was short, and the Lord forgives nothing twice.
Your servant in eternity,
Veneric Soll
From Steward Veneric Soll to Reeve Harl Bassett, by raven

Steward Soll,
Three families slipped into the reeds before dawn, the Marles and Pikes among them, gone the moment the tithe bell rang. Send hounds and men enough to beat the marsh; we cannot spare the watch we keep. The cart axle is rotten besides and threatens to break under the next load.
Your obedient reeve,
Harl Bassett
From Reeve Harl Bassett to Steward Veneric Soll, by raven

Petra,
Have you seen the steward's ledgers this quarter? Column after column, counted twice and initialed thrice, as if one missing hen might undo the whole house. Dour little man. I hear he weighs the tithe grain himself, and trusts no clerk to carry the scale.
Yours in idleness,
Ysolde
From Lady Ysolde Crane to Dame Petra Ashcombe, by hand

Aldric,
Strange news from the steward's tower: he no longer writes his tallies plain. His maid says he has taken to an alphabet of his own devising, crossed out and begun again by candlelight. Even the lord seems amused by it, which frightens me more than the ledgers.
Yours,
Petra
From Dame Petra Ashcombe to Lord Aldric Penrose, by hand

Ysolde,
You will laugh: I have dressed this letter in one of our little court tricks, and not one soul at court will trouble to unpick it. I confess I am pleased with my own cleverness, and mean to gloat of it at the feast.
Your admirer in wit,
Aldric
From Lord Aldric Penrose to Lady Ysolde Crane, by hand
The Key

A cipher hides a message inside a rule. A key is the one secret piece of that rule: without it the message is noise, with it the message is plain. The simplest key is a number. Take the Caesar shift: write out the alphabet, then slide it forward by some fixed count, and swap every letter in your message for the one now standing under it. Slide it back by the same count and the message returns. The rule can be public knowledge. The key, how far you slid it, is the only thing that must stay hidden.

key = shift 3 (Suetonius)

plain:  VENI VIDI VICI
cipher: YHQL YLGL YLFL

House Morrow-Veil once believed the wheel itself was the secret, and burned a captured one as a trophy. It changed nothing; a new wheel is carved in an afternoon. The number was the secret all along, and it never left the steward's head.

This is a Caesar cipher, a shift cipher with a fixed offset applied to every letter. Modern cryptography still separates algorithm from key; the same idea underlies AES and password hashing, where the method stays public and only the key stays secret.
Twenty-six letters, one number. Lose the number and you've lost nothing worth losing; lose the key and you've lost everything.
Real ciphers get fancier than this, boy, but every last one still boils down to: what's the key, and who's got it.
The Key Space

Every cipher has a key space: the full list of keys someone could try. A Caesar shift has twenty-six possible values, one of which leaves the message unchanged and so is never used, leaving twenty-five worth trying. Twenty-five is nothing. A patient clerk, let alone a cipher-monk with an hour and a cup of wine, can turn a wheel twenty-five times and read every result. This is the whole weakness of the shift cipher: its key space is so small that brute force costs almost nothing. Any cipher's true strength is measured by how large and how searchable its key space is, not by how clever its rule looks.
The house assumed twenty-six was a wall too high to climb, and rarely bothered to change the shift at all. A single monk with patience proved that twenty-five tries is not a wall. It is an afternoon.

Modern key spaces are measured in bits: a 128-bit AES key has about 3.4 x 10^38 possibilities, far beyond brute force even for governments. A Caesar shift's key space is under 5 bits, smaller than one password character.
Twenty-five guesses. I've drunk more cups than that before breakfast, and I don't recommend either habit.
Small key space is a sickness. Big key space is only a start; you still need the key itself to stay secret.
Frequency Analysis

No language uses its letters evenly. In English, E appears about 12.7 percent of the time, T about 9.1 percent, A about 8.2 percent, and letters like Q and Z hardly appear at all. This unevenness survives a Caesar shift: shift every letter by the same amount and the tallest bar in a letter count moves with it. Count the letters of a shifted message, find the tallest bar, and assume it stands for E; the distance between that bar and E's true place is the shift itself. This method was first described in the ninth century by the scholar al-Kindi, and remains the standard first attack on any cipher that shifts or swaps letters one for one.

tally of a shifted letter (66 total):
J: 12   Y: 7   Q: 5   T: 5   M: 4
J is tallest, so J probably = E
J is 5 steps past E, so shift = 5

The stewards believed changing their wording each season would hide the cipher. It never mattered: whatever words they chose, English still favored E over every other letter, and the tallest bar always gave the shift away.

This is a classic ciphertext-only attack. Modern block and stream ciphers are built so frequency analysis fails: their output should look statistically uniform, hiding any letter's true popularity entirely.
The tallest bar in the tally never lies to you, boy. People do. Numbers, mostly, don't.
This trick only breaks shifts and swaps. Anything cleverer scrambles the tally too, but you have to start somewhere.
Kerckhoffs's Principle

A cipher should stay secure even if your enemy knows exactly how it works down to the last detail; the only thing that must stay secret is the key. Auguste Kerckhoffs wrote this down in 1883. Judged by that rule, ROT13 and Atbash are not ciphers at all, they are tricks with no key. ROT13 always shifts every letter by exactly thirteen, so doing it twice returns the original text, since thirteen plus thirteen is twenty-six. Atbash always reverses the alphabet, A for Z, B for Y, and so on, and is likewise its own reverse. Neither hides anything once you know its name; secret here means only unfamiliar, never protected.

plain:   THE ORDER READS
rot13:   GUR BEQRE ERNQF
atbash:  GSV LIWVI IVZWH
either one, twice, gives plain again

House Morrow-Veil used Atbash for petty court gossip, trusting an old trick to look mysterious. Once the Order simply named the scheme aloud, every note the house had ever sent fell open the same afternoon.

Kerckhoffs's principle is why modern cryptography publishes its algorithms openly and argues about them in public; secrecy lives only in the key. ROT13 itself was popularized on Usenet in the 1980s, to hide spoilers, never to protect anything.
No key, no secret. ROT13 and Atbash are party tricks, not locks, and I'll argue with any fool who calls them ciphers.
Kerckhoffs said it plain in 1883: assume your enemy knows the whole method already. Only the key gets to hide.
Real locks have moving parts I haven't shown you yet, boy. These two don't. That's rather the point of starting here.
Isaak wakes to iron and candlelight, the chain cold against his wrists.
Awake. Good. I have read the Order's reports on you, and I find I do not believe half of them.
Then ask about the other half. I'll even answer, for a price.
You want blood. I offer ink instead, and paper enough for the truth, however long it runs.
Water first. My throat's full of dust, and I've a story that wants telling properly.
Water, then. I want the method, Isaak Varr, not the myth the Quill likes to tell about itself.
The method. Fine. It starts in Hollowmere, the autumn I was nineteen, before I knew what I was.
Begin.
The reeds hiss in the wind off Blackwater ford. A boy crouches beside a one-eyed monk with a sling.
You've missed the last three.
Shut your mouth and watch the sky, boy.
The sling cracks. A raven drops out of the dusk like a stone, a scrap of oilcloth bound to its leg.
That's a Morrow-Veil bird. You'll have the whole house down on us.
Brother Kett, if you please, since we're to be properly introduced over a corpse.
Isaak. What's in the oilcloth?
Orders, boy. Turned to nonsense by a trick of the alphabet, and nonsense again the moment you know the trick.
How do you undo it?
With this, and one number they think is safe because it's only a number. That's called a key, and it's worth stealing.
A number can't be a secret.
Twenty-six of them can, if you're lazy and never change it. Watch the wheel, and I'll show you how lazy men get caught.
Do we change ours?
Every new moon. Brother Ansgar keeps the Order's keys, and he trusts nobody. Not even me. Especially not me.
Now you know what a key is, boy. It's the only thing they're hiding; everything else you're welcome to.
Almost too easy.
Wait till they get lazier still. It only gets worse for them from here.
Three families gone into the reeds, and the reeve wants hounds sent after them like they're game.
Hounds cost money the reeve doesn't have. He's begging, not commanding. Write that down; it matters.
It matters that House Morrow-Veil is running short of frightened people to work its fields.
Twenty-five shifts. My own cousins still trust a wheel with twenty-five shifts, as if laziness were a virtue.
A key space that small is not a lock. It is an invitation, politely worded.
An alphabet of his own devising. What does that even mean?
It means the steward's bored of borrowed tricks and built one of his own. Worse for us, better for the lesson.
Worse how?
No key hiding in a drawer this time, boy. The whole alphabet's the secret now. We'll want frequency, patience, and Hollowmere.
They take the next courier at the ford: a thin thrall named Odo Lusk, a satchel of ravens' orders on his back.
He's shaking. He knows what we are.
He knows what you are, boy. Thirst's up in your eyes already. Don't.
The hunger's a fist round my throat, and here's supper begging for its life.
Drain him.
Spare him; drink Kett's pig's blood instead.
Odo Lusk does not finish his sentence.
I don't remember letting go. Kett does; he tells me after, quietly, like a man reporting weather.
Pig's blood, boy, not his. Drink it slow, let the lad run, and doctor his letter so the blame falls on damp.
Odo runs like the marsh is on fire behind him. Some part of me hopes he keeps running.
Either way, Hollowmere has one less letter reaching House Morrow-Veil tonight.
The Thirst rises faster than Isaak can master it, and the raven-keeper's lantern is too warm, too close, too alive.
I don't remember crossing the yard. I remember the smell, and then I remember nothing kind.
By the time Kett hauls him off, the keeper is on the ground, and the letter is soaked through, dark with more than ink.
Enough! Enough, boy, he's done, let him be!
My hands wouldn't stop. Kett had to stop them for me.
We'll not get that letter now. There'll be another raven, and a harder one, and you'll do better by it.
So. The wheel again, the tally, and two children playing at monks in the reeds. Familiar work.
My cousin used the same key for ninety years. He considered it tradition. I consider it evidence.
You drained the courier. I'd ask if you regret it, but pale-bloods rarely regret the meal, only the mess.
You let the courier run on pig's blood and a doctored letter. Sentiment, from a thing that eats people. Quaint.
And you frenzied besides, on some wretched keeper. The Order's reports were not exaggerating after all.
Tell me of this alphabet the steward is supposedly devising. Did he steal it, or did he build it?
You'll have to let me get there.
Then get there, Isaak Varr. I am not a patient woman, but I am a thorough one.
The Tithe Roll
Drag cipher tiles onto plaintext letters, guided by the frequency histogram.
Look at the tally scroll before you touch a single tile, boy. Some bars are stone, others are dust.
Count every cipher letter the way a hangman counts nooses. The tallest bar in English is almost always E.
Pin your tallest bar to E, then hunt for a short three-letter word that keeps repeating. That is your next lock to pick.

To Reeve Harl Bassett, at Hollowmere, by the Steward's own hand.
The tithe roll for the new moon stands thus. The Marsh Row households owe four measures each, save the Coopers, who owe six for their two grown sons and their mother besides. The millers on the Long Causeway owe five measures and a jar of the old vintage the Lord prefers. The Reed cottages by the water owe three measures each, and Widow Anwen owes but two, her holding being the smallest on the row.
Mark this well, Reeve. Of the last tithe, three jars had turned before they reached the tithe-house, gone black and sour in the heat of the cart. The Lord does not accept spoilage as an excuse, and neither will I. See that the jars are packed in wet moss this time, and see that your carters do not dawdle at the ford to drink what is not theirs to drink.
One name is added to this roll at the Lady's request, and not for the common roll: the girl called Lise, of the eel-trap cottages. She is not to be counted among the household quotas, and no receipt is to be written for her. You will understand me, Reeve, or in time you will.
Your servant in eternity, Veneric Soll, Steward of House Morrow-Veil
From Steward Veneric Soll to Reeve Harl Bassett, by hand
The Signature
Slide the given crib along the cipher until its pattern of repeats fits.
This letter is too short for the tally scroll to save you. Look instead at what a bureaucrat always writes.
A crib is a guess you already trust. Slide it along the cipher until its repeats line up like a key in a lock.
Try the crib hard against the letter's very end, where a man like this always signs his name the same way.
YOUR SERVANT IN ETERNITY
YOUR SERVANT

My lord Casimir, forgive the haste of this hand.\nOur letters are read. Too many carts turned back at the ford, too many hounds waiting where none should wait, and no road to such knowledge but the raven road. I do not know if the reader is monk or renegade, but I know a fool's habit kept too long. From the next new moon I write in a new hand of my own devising, and the old wheel goes into the marsh mud. Say nothing of this to the household.\nYour servant in eternity, Veneric Soll
From Steward Veneric Soll to Lord Casimir Morrow-Veil, by raven
Bigrams in the Marsh
Count letter pairs and triples, not single letters, to crack this flattened cipher.
The tally scroll lies flat this time, boy. Somebody's clerk was told to hide his favorite letter.
Single letters will not save you here. Count pairs and triples instead: some shapes still cannot help repeating.
Find the three-letter shape that turns up more than any other. In English that is almost always one short, common word.

Warden Tallow,\nThe carts turn south at the ford and climb north to the barn's back door, not the front. The hound naps past the midnight bell; a man stands watch on the stair till the dawn. Burn this fast.\nThe clerk, Wat Coln
From the Steward's clerk, Wat Coln, to Warden Mave Tallow, by hand
Monoalphabetic Substitution

A monoalphabetic substitution cipher swaps every letter of the alphabet for another, fixed for the whole message: every E always becomes the same cipher letter, every T another, and so on. The key is the full swap, a permutation of 26 letters. There are 26! (about 4.03 x 10^26, some 88 bits) possible keys, far too many to try by hand. But the swap never changes which letters repeat, so English's own habits survive underneath it. Count the cipher's letters: the one that turns up most is very likely E. Word shapes, doubled letters and short words like THE help finish the rest.

PLAIN:  THE STEWARD KEEPS THE ROLL
CIPHER: ZIT LZTVQKR ATTHL ZIT KGSS

to Z: the same swap, letter by
letter. English uses E about 1
letter in 8. Count the cipher's
commonest letter: it is likely E,
whatever symbol stands for it.

The Steward believed a scrambled alphabet was as good as a hidden one, and kept the same swap roll after roll all season. He trusted the strangeness of the letters, not the key space, and never asked why the same shapes turned up in every tithe roll.

The first known account of frequency analysis comes from al-Kindi, a 9th-century scholar in Baghdad. It is still the first tool a cryptanalyst reaches for against any simple substitution, and the reason no serious modern system hides plaintext by shuffling one alphabet.
Twenty-six keys is nothing. Twenty-six factorial is everything, and it still will not save a fool who reuses his letters.
Real letters wobble more than one tidy example lets on. Short words lie to you. Long ones confess everything, eventually.
Cribs and Known Plaintext

A crib is a guessed piece of plaintext you expect to find somewhere in a message: a greeting, a date, a signature, a phrase a clerk writes out of habit. Slide the guess against the cipher letter by letter. Where the guessed letters and the cipher letters agree on a consistent swap, you may have found part of the key; where they contradict each other, that position is wrong. Formulaic writing is a gift to the reader of another's mail: bureaucracies repeat themselves, and repetition is a crack. The more predictable the sender, the more of his own cipher he gives away for free.

CRIB:   YOURSERVANT
CIPHER: NGXKLTKCQFZ

Both spell the same shape: the 4th
and 7th letters repeat, in the crib
and in the cipher alike (the R and
the matching cipher letter).
Slide the crib until the repeats
line up. That spot is where it
sits, and the swap falls out
letter by letter.

The Steward thought a short letter was safe because it was too short for the frequency scroll to speak. He forgot that he signed every letter the same way, and a signature guessed once could be dragged along any other letter of his that was ever caught.

Bletchley Park's codebreakers leaned on cribs from formulaic Enigma traffic: routine weather reports and the daily habit of signing off with 'nothing to report'. A predictable sender is every attacker's favorite kind of correspondent, then or now.
Give me one line you always write and I will read every letter you ever send. Habit is a key left in the lock.
A crib does not solve the cipher. It just tells you where to push first, and pushing well is most of the trade.
Bigrams and Trigrams

A bigram is a pair of letters, a trigram a run of three. Even when a clerk flattens single-letter counts on purpose, the pairs and triples that make up ordinary words survive, because whole words still sit next to each other in the same order. In English, TH, HE, IN, ER and AN are the commonest bigrams; THE, AND and ING are the commonest trigrams. Count them across the cipher, word breaks or not, and the shapes of real language show through the disguise: which cipher letters tend to sit beside which others, and in what order, is a fingerprint no single swap can scrub away.

PLAIN TRIGRAM:  THE (9 times)
CIPHER TRIGRAM: ZIT (9 times)

Count every run of three letters
in the cipher. One shape turns up
far more than any other: ZIT.
In English the commonest trigram
is almost always THE, so ZIT is
very likely THE in disguise.

The clerk was told to write sparing of the commonest letter and thought that duty done. He never thought to break up his own favorite little words, and THE sat inside his careful letter as often as it ever had, waiting to be counted.

Modern language models are built on the same idea taken much further: predicting the next letter, word or token from the ones around it. Every autocomplete on your phone is a distant descendant of counting THE against AND.
Flatten the letters all you like. The words still hold hands with their neighbors, and neighbors talk.
Simplified, mind: real cipher-breakers weigh dozens of common pairs and triples at once, not just the one favorite trigram I keep pointing at.
Hollowmere at night smelled of peat smoke and standing water, and under both, of blood going stale in clay jars.
There. Past the third eel-trap. That's her lantern, if the wind hasn't drowned it.
Wenna Grobb was thin as a reed herself, and just as easy to miss if you didn't know to look.
Brother Kett. You said the new one wouldn't bite.
He hasn't yet. Show him what you carry, Wenna, we haven't got the night.
The Steward's roll. Copied it by candle while the house slept, letter for letter, same as always.
She unrolled it like it might scream if she wasn't careful. Maybe it would, eventually.
Get it to your Order fast. He changes his ledger-keepers like other men change boots, and I don't fancy being caught between.
Nobody's catching anybody tonight. Isaak, mind the reeds, and mind your teeth.
I minded them. That night, at least.
Wenna's finger stopped on the fourth line before I'd even finished reading the cipher aloud.
That name. Read it again.
One small name, added at the Lady's request, not for the common roll.
Lise. That's my sister's girl. Eight years old, and light on her feet, and she thinks I don't worry.
Wenna.
Don't. Don't tell me it's nothing. I know what 'not for the common roll' means in this house.
I didn't know, not truly, not yet. I only knew she wasn't crying, and that frightened me more than tears would have.
Then we work faster. That's the only answer either of us has got tonight.
Read that last part again.
'Our letters are read.' He knows, Kett. Or he suspects enough to matter.
Then the clock's already turned over once. He'll change his hand, and we'll be chasing a new alphabet by the next moon.
Small comfort, that we frightened him first.
Small comfort's the only kind Hollowmere hands out. Take it.
'Your servant in eternity.' He signed that on tithe rolls and threats alike. Vanity dressed as devotion.
A signature is a habit wearing a crown. He gave you the same six words every time, and thought it made him sound eternal.
It made him easy to read, is what it did.
Yes. That too. Immortals are terrible at noticing their own repetitions, Isaak. Remember that, chained or not.
Blackwater ford, the barn's back door, a hound that slept past midnight. Kett read it back twice, like he didn't trust his own eyes.
He wrote around his own most common letter and still couldn't help himself. Wrote 'the' nine times in a letter about hiding things.
So you know the route now.
We know the route. Knowing where the cart goes and knowing where Lise sleeps are two different maps, Wenna.
Find both, then.
Wenna held out her wrist before I'd even asked. Her hand shook so hard the lantern light jumped with it.
Take it. You're hungrier than you're letting on, and I'd rather it was you than something worse in the reeds.
I could smell it over the marsh, over the blood already spoiling in the Steward's jars. Everything else went quiet.
She's shaking harder than the cold explains. Word travels fast in a marsh this small, about what you did to Odo Lusk.
She trusts you more than she should, probably. Word of Odo Lusk walking home free travels just as fast as the other kind.
'It's your choice, not mine,' I told her. It wasn't much of a promise. It was all I had.
The Thirst wanted her wrist more than it had wanted anything else all night.
Drink from her wrist
Refuse her offer
He drank. Wenna's breath caught, then eased, like something old and terrible had finally been paid its due.
He let her hand fall, gently, and stepped back before hunger could argue with him.
Whatever happens to that girl Lise isn't a promise either of us can make from a marsh at midnight.
I didn't ask for a promise. I asked you to be quick, and careful, and to come back.
We'll be quick. Careful's asking a lot of him, but I'll vouch for both of us.
It was the closest thing to an oath either of us gave her that night, and it was Kett's, not mine.
The hound smelled me before I smelled it, and by then it hardly mattered which of us moved first.
He struck before Kett could get his name out, teeth first, thought a distant second.
Isaak! Isaak, stop, please-
I heard her like she was shouting from the bottom of a well. The letter went out of her hand into the mud, and I didn't care.
Kett hauled him back by the collar, hard as a man dragging a dog off a kill, and swore the whole while.
That's enough! That's ENOUGH, Isaak, look at me, look at my one damned eye and nobody else's blood.
The handler didn't die. I want that said plainly, for whatever plainness is worth after a thing like that.
Wenna's copy was ruined past reading, soaked through with mud and worse. We'd have to catch the Steward's next letter clean.
A crib. Elegant. You didn't break his alphabet so much as let him hand you the last six words of every letter he ever wrote.
He handed us more than that, eventually.
Vanity, Isaak. 'Your servant in eternity' is not devotion, it is a man admiring the sound of his own permanence.
You drank from the courier girl. I wonder if you tasted her fear, or only her blood.
You refused her. Interesting. Hunger is not usually so polite.
And a hound's handler nearly died for your restraint failing once. The ledger remembers that too.
Ask what you actually want to ask.
Very well. How did the many-toothed key fall into a monk's hands, Isaak? Keys like that are not lost. They are given, or stolen.
The Steward Grows Clever
Five wheels turn together. Find each column's peak and set the drums.
Five teeth, five families. Split the letters by their place in the row before you stare at any of them.
Each family is just a shift wearing a mask. Read its tallest bar as E and the drum falls into place.
Set one drum at a time and watch the scroll; it will tell you the moment a column reads true.

Warden Tallow,

The Lord sends a new cipher from his own library, five teeth to its wheel. Use it from this day.

The carts cross at Blackwater ford after moonrise. Count them twice and say nothing to the reeve.

Your servant in eternity,
Veneric Soll
From Steward Veneric Soll to Warden Mave Tallow, by raven
Kasiski's Lens
Measure the gaps between repeated letters to learn how many teeth this key has.
Look for the same three letters showing up twice in a message this long. That is never an accident.
Measure the distance between each repeat. The key's length divides most of those numbers.
Take the common factor of your spacings, split the text into that many columns, then read each peak.

Steward,

You try my patience. The tithe is not a suggestion, and Hollowmere is not exempt from it. Twice the tithe came short, and twice you blamed the reeve, the weather, the carts.

Collect the tithe at Hollowmere before the new moon, or find yourself replaced before the new moon after that.

Blood is owed, blood is paid, world without end.

Hollowmere remembers its tithe even when its steward forgets his sums, and the new moon does not wait on excuses. Recite it until you believe it. Blood is owed, blood is paid, world without end.

See the tithe is whole.

Casimir Morrow-Veil
From Lord Casimir Morrow-Veil to Steward Veneric Soll, by raven
The Loom of Columns
Too short for repeats to help. Slide the loom until the strands look like English.
Nothing repeats twice in a note this short. Don't waste an hour hunting for a pattern that isn't there.
Split the letters into strands and test each width. English strands clump; a wrong width scatters.
Find the width where the vial reads truest, then read each strand's tallest bar as E.

Tallow,

Word from the manor: the night has moved. Bring the carts before dusk falls, not after moonrise as before. The old crossing floods whenever it rains, so use the north path this time and go quietly. Burn this note once you have read it.

Soll
From Steward Veneric Soll to Warden Mave Tallow, by hand
Bit Rosary
Flip the beads that differ, then pour the byte twice to find the key.
A bead only knows heads or tails. Flip the ones where your two rows don't agree.
Pour the same key over the sum twice and it cancels itself out. That is the whole trick of it.
Once you have one letter, turn the dial through all its settings and keep whichever reads most like English.
BLOOD
They watch the north gate after dark now. Do not use the old path again, and burn this once you have read it.
From an unnamed thrall of Hollowmere, passed hand to hand
The Litany Key
Find the key's length on the comb, then tune each strand to its truest English.
A prayer repeated is still a prayer. Somewhere in this cipher, the same words keep answering themselves.
Compare blocks of bytes against each other. The size where they agree most is the key's length.
Split the bytes into that many strands and turn each dial until its strand scores like English.

Casimir Morrow-Veil,

Our friend in the Quill is worth ten spies. He sits among the cipher-monks and copies their manifests before the ink is dry, and for a purse of silver and a promise of turned blood he tells us which routes the Order walks and which raven-roosts they watch.

He calls himself devout. He is merely for sale, which is a kind of devotion I understand far better than prayer.

Through him we know the Order reads more of our mail than either of us would like, and that they have not yet broken the new cipher. Use that ignorance while it lasts. Do not write his name where a courier might read it.

Your servant in eternity,
Veneric Soll

The Vigenere Cipher: many locks, one dull key

A Vigenere cipher is many Caesar shifts interleaved, one for each letter of a keyword. Write the key under the message, repeating it to length; each plaintext letter shifts by its key letter beneath it. A five-letter key means five separate shift ciphers, laced together column by column. It was first described by Giovan Battista Bellaso in 1553, though history gave the credit to Blaise de Vigenere, who came later. For nearly three centuries the court called it le chiffre indechiffrable, the unbreakable cipher. It is not unbreakable. It only asks a patient reader to notice that the key itself repeats.
PT  ATTACKATDAWN\nKEY LEMON\nCT  LXFOPVEFRNHR

House Morrow-Veil trusted a single clever word to guard every letter for a season. They changed the wheel once and then trusted it, as if cleverness bought silence forever. It did not; it only bought time, and time is what the Order had plenty of.

Modern ciphers still fear a repeating key. A stream cipher that reuses its keystream, or a block cipher run in a mode that behaves like one, leaks exactly the way this one does: patterns in the key become patterns in the world.
Five wheels, not five secrets. Same trick five times over, wearing five different hats. Don't let it scare you, boy.
I'm rounding here: the real fight was who wrote it first, some Italian or some Frenchman. Doesn't change how you crack it.
Kasiski's Lens: measuring the gaps

If the same three or four letters appear twice in a Vigenere ciphertext, it is usually because the same plaintext letters lined up with the same stretch of key, some whole number of key-lengths apart. Measure the distance between each repeat, and the key's true length will divide most of those distances. Short repeats can happen by pure chance, so trust trigrams and longer, and trust a pattern that shows up more than once. Friedrich Kasiski published this attack in 1863. Charles Babbage broke Vigenere ciphers by a similar method roughly a decade earlier, but he never published his work, so his name waited a century for credit.

The steward believed a long enough message could never repeat itself by accident, so he never varied his key mid-letter. Patience alone unravelled him; the repeats were sitting in plain sight the entire time.
The same idea drives modern traffic analysis: repeated patterns in encrypted data, even without breaking the cipher itself, tell an analyst about structure, timing, or reused keys underneath.
Coincidences happen. Two repeats might be luck. Ten repeats at the same spacing is a confession.
Babbage did this first and told nobody. A monk who doesn't publish is a monk who gets forgotten.
Index of Coincidence: the shape of a language

Every language has a fingerprint: some letters turn up far more often than others, so two letters drawn at random from real English are more likely to match than two drawn from gibberish. The index of coincidence measures that odds of a match: IC equals the sum of each letter's count times one less than itself, divided by the text's length times one less than itself. Ordinary English scores near 0.066 to 0.067. Purely random letters score near 0.038. Split a Vigenere ciphertext into the wrong number of columns and each column still looks random. Split it into the right number, matching the key's length, and every column suddenly looks like English again. William Friedman formalised this measure in 1922.

The index of coincidence still helps modern analysts fingerprint a language or detect that two supposedly random streams are secretly related, long before anyone reads a single decrypted word.

Bits, Bytes and the Chalice: what XOR is

Every letter the alchemists write becomes a byte, eight little beads that are each either lit or dark. XOR compares two beads and lights the result only when exactly one of them was lit; two dark or two lit beads both go dark. Flip the same bead twice with the same key and it returns to where it started, because a thing XORed with itself vanishes, and a thing XORed with darkness stays itself. XOR is its own undoing, which is exactly why the Court's alchemists love it: one chalice pours the cipher on, and the very same chalice, poured again, pours it back off. The bead widget on this page lets you pour it yourself.

The alchemists assumed a chalice poured twice was twice as strong. It is not; poured twice with the same key, it undoes itself completely, which is a lesson in arithmetic dressed up as a lesson in wine.
XOR is the workhorse of real ciphers too: stream ciphers, block-cipher modes and one-time pads all lean on the same self-cancelling trick to combine key and message.
A XOR A is nothing. Pour the same wine into the same cup twice and you're back where you started.
I'm simplifying the beads to eight per letter. Real machines sometimes use bigger words, but the pouring works the same.
The Single Chalice: one key, two hundred fifty six guesses

Pour one single key-byte over an entire message and you get single-byte XOR, which is nothing more than a Caesar cipher wearing bytes instead of letters. There are only two hundred fifty six possible keys, few enough to try every single one. For each candidate key, undo the pour and ask how English the result looks: common letters common, spaces where you expect them, no strings of nonsense. Score every candidate that way and the true key stands out from the noise, the same as reading the tallest bar of a frequency chart once told you which shift was Caesar's.

PT  MEET AT DUSK
KEY one byte, 0x2B
CT  666E6E7F0B6A7F0B6F7E7860
try all 256, score English

The Court believed one key-byte poured over a whole message was safe simply because there were hundreds of choices. Two hundred fifty six is a crowd to a man guessing blind, and nothing at all to a scale that scores every guess at once.

This exact technique, scoring every single-byte key by letter frequency, is a standard first exercise in modern cryptography training, because it teaches the scoring habit every later attack in this game reuses.
Two hundred fifty six keys. Count them on your fingers forty times, or let the gauge do it.
Same trick as reading the wheel's tallest bar as E. Bytes just make it look scarier.
The Litany Key: Vigenere in bytes

Repeat a short key over and over and XOR it against a long message, byte by byte, and you have built the same machine as Vigenere, only in bytes instead of letters. Finding the key's length works differently here: measure the Hamming distance, the count of differing bits, between blocks of the ciphertext, divide by the block size, and average across several pairs. The key size giving the smallest normalized distance is usually the true one, since blocks under a matching key line up like English lines up with itself. Split the bytes into that many strands; each was XORed with one repeated byte, so it falls to the same single-chalice attack.

This attack is the classic first step against repeating-key XOR in real cryptanalysis exercises, and the same Hamming-distance trick appears whenever an analyst suspects two supposedly independent streams share a hidden period.
Hamming distance just counts where two things disagree, bit for bit. Nothing mystical about it.

The One-Time Pad: a key you must never repeat

A one-time pad is unbreakable, but only under conditions nobody's house ever quite manages: a truly random key, as long as the message, kept secret, and never used twice. Reuse it once and the magic that made it perfect becomes the flaw that breaks it. XOR two messages under the same pad and the pad cancels out entirely, leaving the XOR of the two plaintexts, no key required. Guess a likely word in one message, XOR that guess against the stream, and fragments of the other message spill out wherever the guess was right. Shannon proved the perfect-secrecy conditions in 1949; the Soviets broke their own rule, and codebreakers spent decades reading the consequences.

P1 ATTACKS  P2 ATTIRES
same pad; C1 xor C2 = P1 xor P2
guess P1, xor result gives P2
wrong guess yields only garbage
The Order assumed any two intercepted letters must hide two different secrets. A shared, reused key ties them together instead, so cracking one crib into the stream cracks a second letter for free.

This exact failure sank Soviet intelligence traffic in the VENONA program of the 1940s. Its modern descendant is nonce reuse in stream ciphers and in AES-GCM, where a repeated nonce leaks the keystream and, in GCM's case, can let a forger fake new messages entirely.
A pad used once is a vault. A pad used twice is a diary somebody left open.
Perfect secrecy needs a truly random key as long as the message. Real houses almost never manage all four conditions at once.
VENONA took codebreakers years to crack open, and it only worked because the Soviets got lazy first. Laziness is the whole lesson of this act.
